author: BrentDesk Research
headline: Diriyah sends its chief projects officer to Saudi Mega Projects
deck: Two Diriyah executives appear on the Riyadh agenda, covering the gap between what a heritage district is meant to be and what can actually be built.
excerpt: Diriyah Company sends both Matthew Boot, chief projects officer, and Josep Forroll, chief development strategy officer, to Saudi Mega Projects in Riyadh.
content:
Diriyah Company appears twice on the Saudi Mega Projects agenda in Riyadh at the end of September: Matthew Boot as chief projects officer and Josep Forroll as chief development strategy officer. Sending both signals of a programme where strategy and delivery are still actively negotiating with each other.

Diriyah is the hardest of the Saudi giga-projects to build, and the reason is architectural rather than logistical. The development is anchored on At-Turaif, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and its design language is mud-brick Najdi vernacular executed at modern scale. That combination imposes constraints that a conventional tower programme does not face: traditional construction methods that must satisfy contemporary structural and fire codes, finishes that resist industrial standardisation, and a heritage buffer that limits what can be done on adjacent land.

This publication has reported the specific version of that problem — that a museum is a harder contract than the hotels that built Diriyah's programme. Cultural buildings carry environmental control requirements, security specifications and fit-out tolerances that hospitality construction does not, and they are typically procured later in a programme when the contractor market is already committed elsewhere.

The chief projects officer's presence on a delivery platform is therefore more interesting than a chief executive's would be. Delivery executives talk about sequencing, contractor capacity and the packages currently in the market, which is the information the supply chain attends these events to obtain. Diriyah has been a substantial buyer of Saudi contracting capacity and this publication has covered its contract awards, including the Samoca package with Albawani and Hassan Allam.

The strategy side has a different question to answer. Diriyah's commercial model depends on the district functioning as a destination — hotels, retail, cultural venues and residential drawing visitors and residents into an area that was, until recently, peripheral to Riyadh's centre of gravity. That requires the whole assembly to open in a coherent sequence, because a heritage district with a completed hotel and an unfinished public realm does not work as either.

Both officers appear alongside delivery leads from Red Sea Global, King Salman Park, New Murabba and Expo 2030, and the comparison across programmes is where the conference earns its value: these organisations are drawing on the same Saudi contractor base, the same imported specialist trades and the same window before the Expo 2030 and World Cup 2034 deadlines.

Speaker names and titles come from the organiser's published agenda. Diriyah has been among the more consistent Saudi clients in bringing packages to market, and the contractor community reads its award cadence closely.
